domains.title: The August Rice Spirit
domains.subtitle: Heavenly Grandson and Bearer of the Regalia
domains.lead: Ninigi is the grandson of Amaterasu, sent from heaven to rule the terrestrial world and establish the imperial line. He descended to Takachiho in Kyūshū bearing the Three Sacred Regalia — the mirror, the sword, and the jewel — and his great-grandson became Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor of Japan.

cards.name: Bearer of the Regalia
cards.desc: He carried the mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi, and the jewel Yasakani from heaven to earth — the warrant of every later throne.

cards.name: Heavenly Descent
cards.desc: Amaterasu sent him to rule the land of reed plains — the tenson kōrin, the founding descent of Japanese sovereignty.

cards.name: Imperial Ancestor
cards.desc: His line produced Hoori, Ugayafukiaezu, and Jimmu — four generations from heaven to Kashihara.

cards.name: Rice Spirit
cards.desc: His name's final character, 芸, ties him to rice and skill — agricultural sovereignty in a single syllable.

mythology.lead: Ninigi's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly realm of Amaterasu and the earthly rule of the emperors: four scenes — the descent, the negotiated surrender of the land, the ordeal by fire that proved his wife's fidelity, and the genealogy that produced Jimmu — suffice to carry three regalia and a nation from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Kashihara.

myths.title: The Descent from Heaven
myths.text: When Amaterasu resolved that the land of reed plains should be governed from heaven, she chose not her son but her grandson. She gave Ninigi the Three Sacred Regalia — the mirror Yata, the sword Kusanagi that Susanoo had won from the eight-forked serpent, and the curved jewel Yasakani — and sent him down, escorted by the deities Ame-no-koyane and Futodama, from the Floating Bridge of Heaven to Takachiho in Kyūshū. The Kojiki (Book I) frames the descent as a transfer of title: heaven holds sovereignty, and the earth must receive it. One detail sharpens the stakes. As Ninigi left, Amaterasu told him the mirror was to be worshipped as her own spirit — the warrant of his rule was simultaneously her presence. A thousand generations of imperial ideology condensed into a single instruction: the emperor rules because he carries what Ninigi carried. The myth means that legitimacy, in the Japanese telling, is a thing handed down, not taken.

myths.title: Ōkuninushi's Withdrawal
myths.text: The earth, however, was occupied. Its master, the great kami Ōkuninushi, had built and governed the land — some say he had won it by ordeal and war — and heaven's envoy could not simply take it. The Kojiki (Book I) tells how Ninigi pressed the matter through negotiation rather than battle, with pressure from the celestial host. Ōkuninushi consulted his sons; his wise son Kotoshironushi, recognising heaven's claim, withdrew of his own accord and is still honored at Mount Miwa. His father then set his price: a great sanctuary built for him at Kizuki in Izumo — the origin of the shrine now called Izumo Ōyashiro — and the keeping of the land's hidden, numinous affairs. In one stroke the myth explains two of Japan's greatest shrines and establishes a template of Japanese statecraft: conquest by diplomacy, and the defeated party honored, not erased. The Nihon Shoki gives variant versions, but the pattern holds. The myth's deepest meaning may be that sovereignty is best taken by leaving the former holder something greater than his loss.

myths.title: The Ordeal of Fire
myths.text: Standing one day at Cape Kasasa, Ninigi saw a woman more beautiful than any other and asked her name. She was Konohanasakuya-hime, daughter of the mountain-god Ōyamatsumi; she consented, and that same night conceived. Ninigi doubted her when the pregnancy showed at once — whose child could be born in a day? The princess answered with fire. She entered a parturition hut, sealed it, and set it alight, vowing that if the children were truly Ninigi's they would be unharmed. In the midst of the flames she delivered three sons: Hoderi, the luck of the sea; Hoori, the luck of the mountains; and Hosuseri. Mother and infants survived, and Ninigi's suspicion was answered with living proof. The episode is one of the most vivid ordeal-births in world mythology, and it quietly elevates the bride: it is her fidelity, tested by fire, that founds the dynasty. The myth means that legitimacy flows not from the doubting husband but through the mother whose truth outlasts the flames.

myths.title: From Ninigi to Jimmu
myths.text: The Nihon Shoki (Books I–III) completes the genealogy. Hoori, the mountain-lucky son, married Toyotama-hime, daughter of the sea-god, and their son Ugayafukiaezu wed his aunt Tamayori-hime; of that union was born Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko, who marched east from Hyūga, fought through the Kumaso, and acceded at Kashihara — Emperor Jimmu, the legendary first emperor. Ninigi is thus Jimmu's great-grandfather, and every imperial genealogy in Japanese history has run through him. The same chapters preserve the succession stories the official line passed over: in one Nihon Shoki variant, Ninigi's elder brother Ame-no-hohi was sent to the earth first and never returned, and Ninigi's descent was the second attempt. The sources are candid that more than one heir was considered. The myth's function is transparent and, for over a millennium, was effectively constitutional: it makes the emperor a descendant of Amaterasu in the fourth generation. It means that the state located its origin not in a conquest but in a birth — a genealogy, not a battlefield.

lore.syncretism: Ninigi was never a popularly worshipped god, and that absence is itself revealing. His role was absorbed into two institutions: the imperial house, which descends from him, and State Shinto, which taught his descent as the founding act of the Japanese nation. In the Meiji period the tenson kōrin became civic doctrine, and Jimmu's traditional accession date anchored the national holiday Kigensetsu. After 1945 the emperor's divinity was renounced, and Ninigi settled back into mythology — taught in schools, visited at Takachiho, but rarely prayed to. Buddhism, meanwhile, largely ignored him: he is one of the few major kami without a Buddhist avatar (honji). His syncretic afterlife is thus mostly political memory — the story a state told about where its authority came from.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ninigi's legacy is carried by objects and places rather than temples. The Three Sacred Regalia he bore — mirror, sword, jewel — remain the symbols of imperial legitimacy, presented at each accession though never publicly displayed. Takachiho in Miyazaki Prefecture, his traditional landing place, draws pilgrims and visitors to the Ama-no-Iwato shrine and the gorge of the descent; Kashihara Jingū in Nara marks where his great-grandson Jimmu is said to have acceded. The Kojiki (712) and Nihon Shoki (720) preserve his story as the hinge between gods and emperors. In a Japan that no longer claims divine descent, Ninigi endures as the mythological explanation of why the islands were long thought to belong to one unbroken line.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ninigi is the moment when heaven touches earth. He carries divine authority not as force but as gift — the mirror that sees truly, the sword that cuts cleanly, the jewel that holds abundance — and his story asks what it means to receive power and pass it on. He is, notably, a mediocre protagonist: he doubts his wife, wins no battles, performs no miracles. The tradition seems uninterested in his character because his function is transmission, not heroism. He is a conduit, and the myth honors the conduit more than the current.

That is a quietly radical theology of legitimacy. Authority is not earned in the descent but entrusted before it, and its proof is not the bearer's virtue but the unbroken line that follows him. Every institution that inherits rather than conquers its mandate — every regency, every relay, every succession — retells Ninigi's descent without knowing it.

lore.archaeology: No artifact can be tied to Ninigi himself, but the geography of his myth is mapped in standing shrines. Takachiho in Miyazaki Prefecture keeps the sites of the descent — the Ama-no-Iwato ('Cave of Heaven') shrine and the sheer gorge where, by tradition, he first set foot on earth. Izumo Ōyashiro in Shimane, rebuilt in its monumental ancient form, marks the sanctuary Ōkuninushi demanded as the price of withdrawing; excavations in 2000 uncovered pillar bases suggesting an ancient structure of unprecedented height. Kashihara Jingū in Nara stands at the foot of Unebi-yama, the traditional accession site of Jimmu, Ninigi's great-grandson. The regalia he carried are kept at Ise (the mirror), Atsuta (the sword), and the palace (the jewel) — none ever displayed or archaeologically examined. Ninigi's material record is thus a landscape of shrines rather than a museum of objects.
